This principle—relevance, association, and distributed encoding—appears in an analogous way in artificial intelligence. The comparison is functional, not architectural. Vector Databases in AI In a vector database, each memory or piece of data is encoded as a high-dimensional vector: a string of numbers that mathematically captures its semantic meaning . On its surface, vector databases seem foreign and complex, in that information is converted into long strings of numbers that, to the human mind without a code key, are largely undecipherable. However, if you step back and consider the underlying function, modern AI vector databases organize and retrieve information in ways that might be understood to conceptually mirror how the brain accesses meaning through associative memory. Rather than being sorted by strict labels or categories, these data points are stored by proximity of meaning in multidimensional space. When you query a vector database, it doesn’t return only the exact match—it returns the closest meanings based on context and learned associations. If traditional databases are a card catalog (exact matches), vector databases are a librarian who knows that king and queen are related not by spelling but by the concept of royalty . Certainly, when we think about the massive web of our neurons in our biological brains firing electrical signals in the storage or retrieval of information, that is as equally nonintuitive as a long string of numbers in a vector database. Similarly, human memory works through associations rather than strict categorization. When we try to recall a fact, we don’t sort through a mental filing cabinet; we activate related concepts, emotional connections, and narrative contexts. Both biological and artificial systems use networks of associations. When we try to recall a fact, we don’t sort through a list alphabetically—we remember related things, emotionally charged moments, stories that stuck. Our brain doesn’t store data in strict files; it creates an interwoven web of meaning, dynamically accessed depending on context. While not architecturally or structurally the same, vector databases offer a conceptual parallel to how the brain organizes memory—by proximity of meaning. The work at our learning company has centered on helping people generate deeply integrated enduring memory with extraordinary efficiency. Understanding how the brain encodes memory has guided both the scientific and technological approaches we’ve taken. And today, we have nearly six billion learner interactions in our platform. This is a giant database of behavior. And the findings from that database are then deeply integrated into our AI training agent and loaded into the AI brain, its vector database. But to fully appreciate this parallel, it helps to look deeper inside the AI itself. In transformer-based neural networks such as ChatGPT, once the input text is tokenized and converted to high-dimensional vectors, it is passed through a series of layered processing blocks—often dozens or even hundreds deep. Each layer contains mechanisms for attention (which allows the model to focus on relevant context) and feed-forward transformation (which distills that context into new representations). You can visualize these layers like stacked systems of filters and pathways—a cascade where each level reinterprets the prior one, enhancing abstraction and refining meaning. At every step, attention flows backward and forward, emphasizing context and forming the basis for predictive reasoning. This structure resembles the cortical feedback loops in the human brain that we talked about in the section called “The Layered Brain” (no, that is just a coconut, not a face), where information flows not just forward from sensory input to higher cognition but also backward, allowing memory, expectation, and intention to shape perception. Feedback loops allow expectations to influence how ambiguous signals are resolved. And aligning with expectations can be more convincing to the brain than reality itself. Similarly, in generative pretrained transformer (GPT) models, early layers might detect sentence structure, while deeper layers infer tone, intent, or even contradiction, feeding back those insights into the unfolding prediction process. Both systems demonstrate that intelligence doesn’t arise from static storage. It emerges from the dynamic interplay of layers, where prediction, context, and memory converge to construct meaning. When GPT completes your sentence, or your brain recalls a childhood memory in the middle of a conversation, the underlying mechanisms—though materially different—are functionally resonant. It’s not that GPT is a brain. It’s that both are systems for layered inference, association, and predictive construction. Each layer refines and reshapes meaning in a way that allows thought—or output—to feel coherent, connected, and alive. And the resulting relational storage in a vector database feels highly analogous to the famous principle about our brains’ storage and retrieval. Based on the foundational work of neuroscientist Donald Hebb, Stanford neuroscientist Carla Shatz coined the memorable phrase: 33 , 34 “Neurons that fire together, wire together.” And that is the point we are trying to grasp here. Both biological and artificial neurons that fire together do indeed wire together to form what we call meaning. Revisiting the Role of Confidence in Human Learning In AI, a “hallucination” occurs when the model produces an answer with an expression of high “confidence,” despite lacking a factual basis. It is striking how efforts to mitigate hallucinations in large language models echo the processes of human learning. We explored how prompting learners on our platform to assess their confidence during learning heightened attention and dramatically improved understanding and retention of new knowledge. This metacognitive act required engagement of the amygdala—the brain region linked to emotional salience and decision-making that we talked about—effectively priming the brain to pay closer attention and integrate learning more deeply. Researchers had to train the AI by modeling the idea that it was acceptable for the AI not to know, introducing a form of internal “confidence” estimation.
